specStatements.text: When a force causes an object to move through a distance work is done on the object. So a force does work on an object when the force causes a displacement of the object.
The work done by a force on an object can be calculated using the equation:
work done = force × distance (moved along the line of action of the force)
work done, W, in joules, J
One joule of work is done when a force of one newton causes a displacement of one metre.
Students should be able to describe the energy transfer involved when work is done.
Students should be able to convert between newton-metres and joules.
Work done against the frictional forces acting on an object causes a rise in the temperature of the object.

concepts.definition: Work is done on an object when a force causes the object to move through a distance, that is when the force causes a displacement of the object. A force that produces no displacement does no work, however large the force is and however long it is applied for.

concepts.term: Distance moved along the line of action of the force
concepts.definition: The distance s used in the work equation is the distance the object moves along the line of action of the force, not simply any distance it travels. Movement at right angles to the force contributes nothing to the work done by that force.

work done = force × distance (moved along the line of action of the force), written in symbols as W = F s, where work done, W, is in joules, J; force, F, is in newtons, N; and distance, s, is in metres.
The unit of work done and of energy. One joule of work is done when a force of one newton causes a displacement of one metre.

Force in newtons multiplied by distance in metres gives work in newton-metres. The newton-metre and the joule are the same size of unit: 1 joule = 1 newton-metre, so a value in N m converts to the identical number of J.

concepts.term: Energy transfer when work is done
concepts.definition: Doing work is a way of transferring energy. When a force does work on an object, energy is transferred to that object, and the amount of energy transferred in joules is equal to the work done in joules.
When an object moves against frictional forces, work is done against those forces. The energy transferred is not lost: it raises the temperature of the object rather than making it move faster.

Work done against the frictional forces acting on an object causes a rise in the temperature of the object, so surfaces such as brake blocks, rubbed hands and dragged crates become warmer as they move.

misconceptions.question: A shopper stands still holding a heavy bag for two minutes. Is work done on the bag?
misconceptions.correct: No work is done on the bag, because the upward force causes no displacement of the bag.
misconceptions.misconception: It feels like hard effort, and I am holding with a big force, so work must be being done.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday English 'work' means effort, and holding or straining is tiring, so students judge work by how hard the task feels rather than by whether the object moves.
misconceptions.correction: Work is done only when a force causes a displacement. With no movement s = 0, so W = F × 0 = 0 J however tiring the task is.

misconceptions.question: A machine does 6000 N m of work. What is this in joules?
misconceptions.correct: 6000 J, because 1 joule = 1 newton-metre, so the number is unchanged.
misconceptions.misconception: Newton-metres and joules are different sizes, so I must multiply or divide by 1000 (or 10) to change between them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Nearly every other conversion students meet (mm to m, g to kg, kJ to J) uses a factor of 10, 100 or 1000, so they expect a numerical factor here too.
misconceptions.correction: The newton-metre and the joule are two names for the same unit: 1 joule = 1 newton-metre. Only the words change, so 6000 N m = 6000 J.

misconceptions.question: A waiter walks 5 m across a room holding a tray level. Does the upward force on the tray do work?
misconceptions.correct: No, because the tray moves at right angles to the upward force, so it moves no distance along the line of action of that force.
misconceptions.misconception: The tray definitely moved 5 m, so the distance in W = F s is 5 m and work has been done.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read 'distance' as any distance travelled and ignore the bracket in the specification equation, which specifies distance moved along the line of action of the force.
misconceptions.correction: Only the distance moved along the line of action of the force counts. Horizontal movement is at right angles to a vertical force, so s = 0 for that force.

misconceptions.question: A force of 25 N moves a trolley 8 m. What is the work done?
misconceptions.misconception: You divide the force by the distance (or the distance by the force) to get the work done.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Many GCSE equations students meet, such as speed = distance ÷ time and density = mass ÷ volume, are divisions, so division becomes the default operation when two numbers are given.
misconceptions.correction: W = F s is a multiplication: work done = force × distance. Dividing gives 3.125 or 0.32, neither of which is the work done.

misconceptions.question: A force of 40 N is applied to a box. What unit is the work done measured in?
misconceptions.correct: Joules, J. Force is measured in newtons, but work done is measured in joules.
misconceptions.misconception: Work is caused by a force, so work must also be measured in newtons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The force is usually the number quoted in the question, and students carry its unit through to the answer without applying the equation, blurring the quantity force with the quantity work.
misconceptions.correction: In W = F s, force, F, is in newtons, N, and work done, W, is in joules, J. A force value on its own is never an amount of work.

misconceptions.question: A 40 N force is applied to a box for 15 s while the box stays still. What is the work done?
misconceptions.correct: 0 J, because the distance moved is zero; the time for which the force acts is not used in W = F s.
misconceptions.misconception: The 15 s is the other number in the question, so it must be the s in W = F s.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The symbol s is used for seconds as a unit and for distance as a quantity, and students pick whichever second number the question supplies.
misconceptions.correction: In W = F s the symbol s stands for distance in metres, not for time. Time never appears in the work done equation.

misconceptions.question: What is the definition of one joule of work?
misconceptions.correct: One joule of work is done when a force of one newton causes a displacement of one metre.
misconceptions.misconception: One joule is the work done when a force of one newton acts for one second.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students confuse the symbol s for distance with the abbreviation s for seconds, and they associate 'per second' definitions with the joule because of its link to the watt.
misconceptions.correction: The joule is defined through distance, not time: 1 N acting through a displacement of 1 m does 1 J of work. Energy per second is power, in watts.

misconceptions.question: A crate is dragged across a rough floor at a steady speed. What happens to the energy transferred by the work done against friction?
misconceptions.correct: It is transferred to the thermal store of the crate and floor, raising their temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: The energy is used up or destroyed by the friction, so it is simply lost.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language talks about 'using up' energy and about friction 'wasting' it, and students cannot see where the energy has gone because nothing appears to happen.
misconceptions.correction: Energy is transferred, never destroyed. Work done against the frictional forces acting on an object causes a rise in the temperature of the object.

misconceptions.question: Why do bicycle brake blocks become hot when the bicycle is braked?
misconceptions.correct: Work is done against the frictional forces at the blocks, which causes a rise in their temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: Friction only slows things down; the warmth comes from the surrounding air rather than from the rubbing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Friction is first taught purely as a force that opposes motion, so its heating effect is treated as a separate, unrelated fact.
misconceptions.correction: The same frictional force that opposes the motion also has work done against it, and that work raises the temperature of the object.

misconceptions.question: A crane lifts a beam. What happens to the energy as work is done on the beam?
misconceptions.correct: Energy is transferred to the beam by the force doing work on it.
misconceptions.misconception: The crane creates new energy and gives it to the beam.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students hear that doing work 'gives' an object energy and read that as making energy, especially where a fuel or a motor is involved.
misconceptions.correction: Doing work transfers energy from one store to another. The joules gained by the beam were already in another store; none are made.

misconceptions.question: A force of 25 N moves a trolley 8 m. A student answers 33 J. What has gone wrong?
misconceptions.correct: They added the force and the distance instead of multiplying them; W = 25 × 8 = 200 J.
misconceptions.misconception: You combine the force and the distance by adding or subtracting them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Under time pressure students combine the two given numbers with the easiest operation, and adding unlike quantities is not obviously wrong to them.
misconceptions.correction: Force and distance have different units and cannot be added or subtracted. The equation is a product: work done = force × distance.

misconceptions.question: W = 3000 J and F = 250 N. How is the equation rearranged to find s?
misconceptions.correct: s = W ÷ F, giving s = 3000 ÷ 250 = 12 m.
misconceptions.misconception: Rearranging W = F s gives s = F ÷ W, or you just multiply W by F.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students rearrange by moving symbols around by eye rather than by dividing both sides, so the two quantities on the right are easily swapped.
misconceptions.correction: Dividing both sides of W = F s by F gives s = W ÷ F. Check by substituting back: 250 × 12 = 3000 J.

misconceptions.question: In W = F s, what does the symbol W stand for and what unit does it take?
misconceptions.correct: W stands for work done and is measured in joules, J.
misconceptions.misconception: W means watts, so the answer to a work calculation is in watts.
misconceptions.whyItArises: W is used as the abbreviation for the watt as well as the symbol for work done, and both appear in the same energy topic.
misconceptions.correction: Here W is the quantity work done, in joules, J. The watt is the unit of power, which is energy transferred per second.

mcqs.stem: In which of these situations is work done on the object by the force described?

options.text: A sledge is dragged forwards and slides 5 m over snow
options.rationale: The pulling force causes a displacement of the sledge along its own line of action, so work is done on the sledge.

options.text: A cleaner pushes hard on a crate that does not move
options.rationale: A large force is applied, but there is no displacement, so no work is done on the crate.

options.text: A waiter carries a tray level across a room
options.rationale: The tray moves horizontally, at right angles to the upward force, so it moves no distance along that force's line of action.

options.text: A student holds a bag of books still for a minute
options.rationale: Holding is tiring but the bag does not move, so the upward force does no work on it.

mcqs.stem: A student holds a box of weight 40 N still at chest height for 15 s. How much work does the student's upward force do on the box?

options.rationale: This is 40 × 15, using the time in seconds as if it were the distance in metres.

options.text: 0 J
options.rationale: The box has no displacement, so s = 0 and W = 40 × 0 = 0 J.
This is 40 ÷ 15, dividing rather than multiplying and still treating the time as a distance.
This quotes the force in newtons as though a force were itself an amount of work in joules.

mcqs.stem: In the equation work done = force × distance, what is meant by the distance?

options.text: The total length of the path that the object takes
options.rationale: Any part of the path at an angle to the force does not count towards the work done by that force.

options.text: The distance moved at right angles to the force
options.rationale: Movement at right angles to a force contributes no distance along its line of action, so it does no work.

options.text: The distance moved along the line of action of the force
options.rationale: The specification defines the distance as the distance moved along the line of action of the force.

options.text: The time for which the force carries on acting
options.rationale: The symbol s stands for distance in metres; time does not appear in the work done equation.

mcqs.stem: A force of 25 N pushes a trolley 8 m along the line of action of the force. How much work is done on the trolley?

options.text: 3.125 joules
options.rationale: This is 25 ÷ 8, dividing the force by the distance instead of multiplying.

options.text: 0.32 joules
options.rationale: This is 8 ÷ 25, the same division carried out the other way round.

options.text: 33 joules
options.rationale: This is 25 + 8; force and distance have different units and cannot be added.

options.text: 200 joules
options.rationale: W = F s = 25 × 8 = 200 J, with the distance measured along the line of action of the force.

mcqs.stem: A crane does 3000 J of work on a load using a force of 250 N. How far does the load move along the line of action of the force?

options.rationale: Rearranging W = F s gives s = W ÷ F = 3000 ÷ 250 = 12 m.
This is 3000 × 250, multiplying the two given values instead of dividing.
This is 250 ÷ 3000, the rearrangement done upside down as s = F ÷ W.
This is 3000 − 250; the equation is a product, so subtraction cannot undo it.

mcqs.stem: Which row gives the correct units for the quantities in W = F s?

options.text: work in newtons, force in newtons, distance in metres
options.rationale: Work done is not measured in newtons; the newton is the unit of force only.

options.text: work in joules, force in newtons, distance in metres
options.rationale: Work done, W, in joules, J; force, F, in newtons, N; distance, s, in metres.

options.text: work in watts, force in newtons, distance in metres
options.rationale: The watt is the unit of power, not of work done; W here is the quantity work done, in joules.

options.text: work in joules, force in newtons, time in seconds
options.rationale: The s in W = F s is a distance in metres, not a time in seconds.

mcqs.stem: A motor does 6000 N m of work. What is this work done in joules?

options.rationale: This multiplies by 1000, as though newton-metres were a thousand times smaller than joules.
This assumes a factor of 10 between the two units; there is no such factor.
1 joule = 1 newton-metre, so the number is unchanged: 6000 N m = 6000 J.

options.text: 6 J
options.rationale: This divides by 1000, treating the conversion like changing joules to kilojoules.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly defines one joule of work?

options.text: The work done when a force of 1 N acts for a time of 1 s
options.rationale: The joule is defined through a displacement, not through a time; energy per second is power.

options.text: The force of 1 N needed to move an object through 1 m
options.rationale: This defines a force rather than an amount of work, and a force is measured in newtons.

options.text: The work done when 1 N of energy is given to a body
options.rationale: Energy is measured in joules, not newtons, so this uses the wrong unit for the energy transferred.

options.text: The work done when a force of 1 N causes a displacement of 1 m
options.rationale: This is the specification definition: one joule of work is done when a force of one newton causes a displacement of one metre.

mcqs.stem: A crane lifts a steel beam steadily upwards. Which statement best describes what happens as the crane's force does work on the beam?

options.text: Energy is transferred to the beam by the crane's force
options.rationale: Doing work is a way of transferring energy; the joules of work done equal the joules transferred to the beam.

options.text: New energy is created by the crane and passed to the beam
options.rationale: Energy cannot be created; the beam's energy comes from another store by transfer.

options.text: Energy is used up by the crane, so none reaches it
options.rationale: Energy is not used up; the work done by the force is exactly the energy transferred to the beam.

options.text: Force is stored inside the beam as it is lifted
options.rationale: Force is not a quantity that can be stored; what the beam gains is energy, in joules.

mcqs.stem: A crate is pushed at a steady speed across a rough floor. What is the main effect of the work done against the frictional forces on the crate?

options.text: The energy transferred is destroyed by friction
options.rationale: Energy is never destroyed; here it raises the temperature of the crate and the floor.

options.text: The temperature of the crate rises steadily
options.rationale: Work done against the frictional forces acting on an object causes a rise in the temperature of the object.

options.text: The kinetic energy of the crate keeps rising
options.rationale: The crate moves at a steady speed, so its kinetic energy store does not change.

options.text: The friction only slows the crate down
options.rationale: Friction opposes the motion, but the work done against it also raises the crate's temperature.

mcqs.stem: A student rubs their hands together quickly and the hands become warmer. Which statement best explains this?

options.text: The movement energy is used up and lost as heat
options.rationale: Energy is not used up; it is transferred to the thermal store of the hands, raising their temperature.

options.text: Warm air trapped between the hands heats them
options.rationale: The warming happens even in cold air; it is the frictional work at the surfaces that raises the temperature.

options.text: Work is done against friction at the hands
options.rationale: Work done against the frictional forces acting on the hands causes a rise in their temperature.

options.text: New heat energy is made by the rubbing
options.rationale: Nothing is made; energy is transferred from the chemical store in the student's muscles.

mcqs.stem: A force does 250 J of work on a trailer as the trailer is pulled along a track. What does this tell you?

options.text: 250 J of new energy was created by the pulling
options.rationale: Doing work transfers energy that already existed in another store; it does not create energy.

options.text: 250 J of energy was used up and cannot return
options.rationale: Energy is transferred rather than used up, and it can be transferred onwards again.

options.text: A force of 250 N acted on the trailer as it moved
options.rationale: 250 J is an amount of work, not a force; the force depends on the distance moved.

options.text: 250 J of energy has been transferred to it
options.rationale: The work done by a force equals the energy it transfers, so the trailer gained 250 J.
